person.name: Konrad_Zuse
person.summary: Konrad Zuse was a German civil engineer, pioneering computer scientist, inventor, and entrepreneur. Working largely in isolation in Berlin and later in postwar Germany, he designed and built the Z1, Z2, Z3, and Z4—some of the earliest programmable, fully automatic, binary floating‑point computers—and created Plankalkül, the first high‑level programming language. In 1949 he founded Zuse KG, one of the first computer companies, and is regarded by many as a father of the modern computer.

chapters.headline: Early Years and Education
chapters.bridge_statement: Covers Zuse’s childhood in East Prussia and Saxony and his broad technical and artistic education culminating in a civil engineering degree in Berlin.

chapters.headline: Independent Inventor in Berlin
chapters.bridge_statement: Traces Zuse’s transition from aircraft engineer to independent inventor in his parents’ Berlin flat, where he created the pioneering Z1, Z2 and Z3 computers and founded his first company during World War II.

chapters.headline: War’s End and Z4 Foundations
chapters.bridge_statement: Follows Zuse’s marriage, escape from Berlin with the Z4, and his efforts in the Allgäu and Göttingen to complete and preserve the Z4, laying the groundwork for postwar commercial computing.

chapters.headline: Zuse KG and Computer Industry
chapters.bridge_statement: Covers the founding and rapid expansion of Zuse KG, the commercial use of the Z4 and later machines, and Zuse’s growing role as a computer entrepreneur until he left management in 1964.

chapters.headline: Later Years and New Ideas
chapters.bridge_statement: Describes Zuse’s post‑management career as consultant, author, and artist, including his speculative work on a computing universe, academic lectures in both German states, and his final years in Hünfeld.

events.title: Birth in Deutsch-Wilmersdorf
events.description: Konrad Ernst Otto Zuse was born on 22 June 1910 in Deutsch-Wilmersdorf, a then-independent locality near Berlin, to Maria and Emil Zuse. His father worked for the postal service, and the family would soon relocate due to his father’s career.

events.title: Family Moves to Braunsberg
events.description: Around 1912, when Konrad Zuse was about two years old, his family moved from the Berlin area to Braunsberg in East Prussia, where his father took a position as a mid-level postal official. Zuse later attended the humanistic Gymnasium Hosianum there, receiving a classical secondary education.

images.caption: Memorial plaque at the former Lyceum Hosianum in Braunsberg (today Braniewo), where Konrad Zuse attended the Gymnasium.

events.title: Transfer to Hoyerswerda Gymnasium
events.description: In 1923 the Zuse family moved again, this time to Hoyerswerda in Saxony. Konrad transferred from the Hosianum in Braunsberg to the Reform‑Realgymnasium in Hoyerswerda, today’s Lessing‑Gymnasium, where he continued his secondary schooling.

images.caption: Assembly hall of the former Konrad‑Zuse‑Gymnasium on Konrad‑Zuse‑Straße 7 in Hoyerswerda, near the school Zuse attended as a teenager.

events.title: Studies at Technische Hochschule Berlin
events.description: After completing school, Zuse enrolled at the Technische Hochschule Berlin‑Charlottenburg (now Technische Universität Berlin). A self‑described “loafer student”, he initially studied mechanical engineering, then switched to architecture, and finally settled on civil engineering. Alongside his studies he worked for almost a year as an advertising illustrator and joined the student fraternity AV Motiv, cultivating both his technical and artistic interests. He graduated as a Diplom‑Ingenieur in civil engineering in 1935.

events.title: Abitur and Early Inventions
events.description: In 1928 Konrad Zuse passed his Abitur in Hoyerswerda, qualifying for university. By this time he had already shown inventive talent: at 14 he had built a coin‑operated “mandarin dispenser” vending fruit and change, and at 18 he constructed a model coal‑loading crane from a Stabil metal construction kit, for which the firm awarded him an honorary certificate.

events.title: Leaves Henschel to Found Workshop
events.description: After receiving his engineering diploma in 1935, Zuse worked briefly as a structural engineer at the Henschel aircraft works in Schönefeld near Berlin. Frustrated by the tedium of manual structural calculations in civil engineering, he soon resigned and set up an inventor’s workshop in his parents’ Berlin apartment. There he began serious work on a machine to automate these calculations, laying the foundations for his first computing machine.

events.title: Builds Mechanical Computer Z1
events.description: Between 1936 and 1938 Zuse designed and built the Z1, a motor‑driven mechanical calculator assembled in his parents’ Berlin living room. The Z1 was the world’s first freely programmable, binary, floating‑point mechanical computer, using punched 35 mm film for program input and possessing separate units for input/output, arithmetic, memory, and control. Financed largely with family and small private support, the machine never ran reliably because of mechanical inaccuracies but encapsulated many concepts of a modern computer.

images.caption: Diagrams from Konrad Zuse’s 1936 patent for a binary mechanical switching element, used in the Z1.

events.title: Completes Relay Prototype Z2
events.description: In 1939 Zuse completed the Z2, an experimental computer that reused the mechanical memory concepts of the Z1 but replaced its unreliable mechanical arithmetic unit with telephone relays. In September 1940 he demonstrated the large relay‑based prototype, which filled several rooms of his parents’ Berlin apartment, to experts from the Deutsche Versuchsanstalt für Luftfahrt in Berlin‑Adlershof. The successful demonstration convinced the aviation research institute to help finance development of Zuse’s next machine, the Z3.

events.title: Founds Zuse Apparatebau in Berlin
events.description: In 1941, in the midst of World War II, Zuse formally founded the firm "Zuse Ingenieurbüro und Apparatebau, Berlin" to develop and build computing machines. Despite wartime controls, his company—employing about 20 staff at its peak—was the only enterprise in Germany permitted to build general‑purpose calculators. The firm’s workshop in Berlin’s Methfesselstraße became the production site for the Z3 and later machines.

events.title: Demonstrates Z3 Computer in Berlin
events.description: On 12 May 1941 Konrad Zuse publicly demonstrated his electromechanical computer Z3 in his Berlin workshop. Built from about 2,600 telephone relays, the Z3 implemented 22‑bit binary floating‑point arithmetic, automatic program control via punched film, and separate memory and arithmetic units. Although it lacked conditional branching in normal use, it is now regarded as the world’s first fully automatic, programmable, working digital computer and, in principle, Turing‑complete.

images.caption: Archival drawing of Konrad Zuse’s Z3 electromechanical computer, completed in Berlin in 1941.

events.title: Develops S1, S2 and Process Control
events.description: From 1942 Zuse, working with Henschel Flugzeug‑Werke, designed the special‑purpose computers S1 and S2 to measure and correct wing profiles for the radio‑guided glide bomb Hs 293. The associated measuring devices implemented some of the first analog‑to‑digital converters. In 1944, at a Henschel facility in Warnsdorf in the Sudetenland, Zuse realized what is considered the first process control by computer, using these systems to automate measurement and control tasks.

events.title: Marriage to Gisela Brandes in Berlin
events.description: On 6 January 1945 Zuse married Gisela Brandes in Berlin, organizing what he later described as a dignified ceremony with carriage, tailcoat, and wedding veil despite wartime conditions. The couple would eventually have five children together, including their eldest son Horst, born later that year, who became a professor of computer science.

events.title: Evacuates Z4 from Berlin to Göttingen
events.description: In early 1945, with Berlin under heavy bombardment, Zuse and his colleagues disassembled the partially completed relay‑based computer Z4 and evacuated it under the cover name V4 by Wehrmacht truck from Berlin to Göttingen. There, in facilities of the Aerodynamische Versuchsanstalt, they completed much of the remaining work even as the front approached, striving to preserve the machine from destruction or capture.

events.title: Resettles in Allgäu with Z4
events.description: After Germany’s surrender, Zuse and his team journeyed south with the disassembled Z4, eventually settling in Hinterstein in the Allgäu. The machine was stored in a flour warehouse in nearby Hopferau. To support his family in the impoverished postwar years, Zuse painted oil pictures of chamois for sale to American tourists and carried out hand calculations for local farmers’ milk accounts—activities sometimes described as Germany’s first digital calculation service—while preparing to rebuild the Z4.

images.caption: The "Konrad Zuse-Haus" in Hinterstein, where Zuse lived and worked on the Z4 after World War II.

events.title: Founds Zuse KG in Neukirchen
events.description: In November 1949 Zuse founded the company Zuse KG in Haunetal‑Neukirchen, Hesse, formalizing his postwar computer business. With the rental income from the Z4 at ETH Zürich and subsequent orders—such as a calculating punch for Remington‑Rand—Zuse KG became one of the earliest dedicated computer firms, setting out to build a family of machines labeled Z11, Z22, and beyond.

images.caption: Building in Haunetal‑Neukirchen used by Konrad Zuse’s company between 1949 and 1957 to manufacture computers.

events.title: ETH Zürich Agrees to Rent Z4
events.description: In 1949 Professor Eduard Stiefel of ETH Zürich traveled to the Allgäu to examine the rebuilt Z4. Impressed by its suitability for scientific computation, he negotiated a rental agreement under which the Z4 would be installed at ETH Zürich’s Institute for Applied Mathematics. This arrangement provided crucial financial support and international recognition for Zuse’s work.

events.title: Z4 Operates at ETH Zürich
events.description: In July 1950 the Z4 was delivered to ETH Zürich, where it became operational as the only working digital computer in continental Europe and, after the BINAC, the second computer in the world to be sold or leased. Used for scientific and engineering calculations—including work on the Grande Dixence Dam—the Z4 ran reliably at ETH until 1955 and inspired the Swiss ERMETH computer project.

events.title: Introduces Electronic Computer Z22
events.description: Around 1955 Zuse KG delivered the Z22, one of Germany’s first commercially successful electronic computers with magnetic‑drum memory. The Z22, following earlier relay‑based models like the Z11, marked Zuse’s transition into fully electronic designs and was sold to universities and industrial customers, strengthening Zuse KG’s position in the emerging computer market.

events.title: Leaves Zuse KG Management
events.description: After years of rapid but financially strained expansion of Zuse KG, Konrad Zuse had to give up his capital shares in 1964 due to over‑indebtedness and withdrew from active management of the firm. He continued to work as a consultant in the computer industry and turned more to theoretical writing and other interests while his company passed into larger corporate ownership.

events.title: Publishes Calculating Space
events.description: In 1969 Zuse published his book "Rechnender Raum" (Calculating Space), proposing that the universe itself could be modeled as a giant cellular automaton or discrete computation. Anticipating later digital physics and simulation‑hypothesis ideas, he argued that physical processes might fundamentally be information‑processing events, extending his computing vision from machines to cosmology.

events.title: Lectures in Ilmenau, East Germany
events.description: In 1983 Zuse, invited privately, gave a public lecture at the Technische Hochschule Ilmenau in the GDR. Although he was not permitted to visit the university’s computing center, the appearance symbolized a rare recognition of his pioneering work in computing across the Cold War divide between West and East Germany.

events.title: Rebuilds Mechanical Computer Z1
events.description: From 1984 to 1989, with support from Siemens and other firms, Zuse led a painstaking project to reconstruct the Z1, which had been destroyed in wartime bombing. Working with assistants, he recreated thousands of mechanical parts and assembled a working replica—now exhibited in Berlin—reviving one of the key milestones of early computer history.

events.title: Death in Hünfeld
events.description: Konrad Zuse died on 18 December 1995 in Hünfeld, Hesse, from heart failure at the age of 85. In retirement he had devoted much of his time to his hobby of expressionist painting, signing his works "Kuno von und zu See". He was buried in Hünfeld, where museums and monuments commemorate his contributions to computing.

images.caption: Grave of Konrad Zuse in Hünfeld, Hesse, where he spent his later years and died in 1995.
